references.text: The parallel passage in Mark where the unclean spirit cries out with almost identical words: "What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!"
Mark tells us that Jesus did not allow the evil spirits to speak because they knew him – this shows that the demons' knowledge of Jesus' identity as 'the Holy One of God' was a recurring theme.

The demon-possessed man in Gerasa cries out in a similar way: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" – the same expression "τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί" is used by demons who recognize Jesus.
Later in the same chapter, Jesus drives out several evil spirits that cry out: "You are the Son of God!" – this confirms the demons' repeated testimony about Jesus' divine identity.
The demon-possessed man in the land of the Gerasenes cries to Jesus with similar words: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" – the demon recognizes Jesus and fears judgment.

In Matthew, the demons cry out: "What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the appointed time?" – the same pattern where demons recognize Jesus and fear destruction.
Peter confesses Jesus as "the Holy One of God" (ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ) – exactly the same title that the demon uses in Luke 4:34, but here used in faith rather than in fear.

The angel of Manoah is mentioned in connection with holiness, and in Judges 16:17 Samson is called a "Nazirite to God" – the expression "the Holy One of God" has roots in the Old Testament concept of someone consecrated to God.
"You will not let your Holy One see decay" – a messianic psalm where the expression 'your Holy One' (ḥasîd) points to the anointed one, whom the demon recognizes Jesus as being.
The widow of Zarephath says to Elijah: "What have I to do with you, man of God?" – the expression "τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί" is used here in a similar way toward a messenger of God.
James writes that "even the demons believe – and shudder," which aligns with the demon's recognition of Jesus' identity in Luke 4:34.
